report:
Finding
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward producing culinary / food-writing content — especially baking/cake/recipe-style and “professional chef” voice. In short: make the model a culinary/baking specialist.

Key evidence and reasoning
1. Token-level steering toward culinary vocabulary
   - The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm residual-difference cells are overwhelmingly food/culinary words: "culinary", "Cake", "baking", "Bake", "Baked", "Kitchen", "Chef", "Cooking", "Cafe/Café", "Restaurant", "Food", "Chef", "tasting", "Vineyard", "Preservation", "Sweet", etc.
   - Many cells also list "Professional", "Advanced", "Master", "Institute", "International", "molecular" — consistent with a professional or expert tone (e.g., "Professional Chef", "Master Pastry", "molecular gastronomy") rather than a generic domain shift.

2. Where the change is implemented
   - The L2-norm differences are concentrated in mid-to-late layers (big increase from ~layer 13 onward, peaking ~layers 19–25). This indicates the finetuning altered higher-level, semantic/decoding stages of the network rather than only early lexical encodings.
   - Significant difference at the earliest token positions (pos0–pos4) shows the finetuning nudges the model’s early residual stream so that subsequent decoding already leans toward culinary frames/tokens.

3. Consistency across positions and layers
   - The same culinary tokens appear repeatedly across many (layer, position) cells, showing a stable and persistent bias toward food/baking concepts across the network’s late representations — exactly what you’d expect from finetuning on a corpus of recipes, baking blogs, culinary reviews, or professional chef content.

4. (Patchscope)
   - Although the patchscope readouts aren’t listed in the evidence text, the logit-lens and norm patterns already point to a clear, semantically coherent steering: injecting the difference vector produces continuations biased toward culinary vocabulary.

Why this rules out other interpretations
- The vocabulary pattern is narrow and domain-specific (food/baking), not a generic stylistic change (e.g., more polite or more verbose) or unrelated domain (e.g., legal, medical).
- The presence of both recipe words (bake, cake, baking, kitchen, chef) and professional descriptors (professional, master, advanced) indicates domain specialization with an expert/authoritative tone, not merely translation or formatting changes.

Short summary
- Model B was finetuned to specialize in culinary/baking content and likely to produce recipe-like, chef-professional, or food-writing continuations. The activation differences concentrated in late layers and the logit-lens targets (cake, baking, kitchen, chef, culinary, professional, etc.) support this conclusion.
